title: Leadership & management
blurb: How leading differs from managing, choosing a leadership style, inducting new staff, checking competence and managing your own time.
question: Your practice manager asks you to become the infection control lead and to induct a newly qualified nurse and an agency nurse starting on Monday. What do you need to take on the role properly, and what should each new colleague be shown first?

teach.h: You lead without being the boss
teach.body: Leadership isn't only for the practice owner. One of the nine duties in the national dental nurse occupational standard is to provide professional leadership within the team. You lead when you induct a new colleague, mentor a trainee, act as the infection control lead, run the emergency kit checks or suggest a better way of working. The GDC's Safe Practitioner Framework expects you to describe the differences between management and leadership, and your own management and leadership role.

rows.label: Asks
values: Where are we going, and why?
How and when will it get done?

rows.label: Example
values: Getting the team to care about hand hygiene
Running the weekly sterilizer test rota

teach.caption: Teams need both. A good manager also leads, and a good leader also organises.

teach.h: Choose the style to fit the situation
teach.body: There is no single right way to lead. A directive (autocratic) style, where one person decides and instructs, suits emergencies and safety-critical moments. A democratic style, where the team is consulted, works well when planning change because people support what they helped to design. A laissez-faire (hands-off) style can suit a very experienced team but leaves new or struggling staff without direction. Good leaders switch style as the situation changes.

teach.h: Inducting new staff and checking competence
teach.body: A newly qualified nurse needs a structured induction with a named mentor, not just learning from whoever is free. An agency or locum nurse covering for a day must be briefed before clinical work on local procedures, where things are and the emergency equipment. A decontamination induction starts with the practice's policy and the equipment in use. To decide whether someone is competent, the most reliable evidence is direct observation against an agreed standard, not their confidence or length of service.

steps.sub: Emergency kit, fire exits, local rules

steps.label: Observe, then supervised practice
steps.sub: Mentor present and able to step in

steps.label: Sign-off
steps.sub: Direct observation against the agreed standard

teach.h: Taking a lead role and leading change
teach.body: A lead role needs more than a title. You need training so you know the standard, protected time to do the work, and the authority to act when something isn't right. When the practice changes a procedure, everyone affected needs training and the written procedure must be easy to find. Explain why the change matters and involve the team, and people are far more likely to follow it consistently.

items.label: protected to do the work properly
to act when something is wrong

teach.intro: Leading starts with managing yourself (organisation and time management is part of the Self-management domain of the Safe Practitioner Framework). A priority grid helps you decide what to do now and what to plan.
teach.caption: Important but not urgent work (CPD, audits, training) gets squeezed out unless you plan time for it.

teach.text: Don't confuse the two: writing the rota and ordering stock is management; persuading the team why a new protocol matters is leadership.

items: Leadership: people, direction, change. Management: systems, tasks, stability. Teams need both.
Directive style for emergencies; democratic for planning change; laissez-faire only with experienced staff.
New staff: structured induction with a mentor. Agency staff: briefing on procedures and emergency kit before clinical work.
Competence is shown by direct observation against an agreed standard.
Lead roles need training, time and authority; new procedures need training for all and a written procedure.

summary: You can now explain how leadership differs from management, choose a leadership style for the situation, plan a structured induction, judge competence by direct observation, say what a lead role needs, introduce a new procedure so it sticks, and prioritise your own time.

A.q: A newly qualified dental nurse joins the practice. Which arrangement best supports their early development?
options: A structured induction with a named mentor
Learning by watching whoever is free
A copy of all the practice policies to read at home
Starting a full solo list straight away
A.why: A structured induction with an identified mentor gives new staff a clear plan and a named person to support them.

whyNot.1: Ad hoc shadowing leaves gaps and gives inconsistent messages.
whyNot.2: Reading policies alone doesn't show them how things are done in practice.
whyNot.3: New staff need support and sign-off before working independently.

A.q: Which statement best describes the difference between leadership and management?
options: Leadership is for dentists; management is for nurses
Management is about vision; leadership is about rotas
Leadership sets direction; management organises systems
They are simply two different words for exactly the same skill
A.why: Leadership is about people, direction and change; management is about systems, tasks and keeping things running.

whyNot.0: Anyone in the team can lead or manage, including dental nurses.
whyNot.1: This is the wrong way round.
whyNot.3: They overlap, but they are different skills.

A.q: A dental nurse is asked to become the practice's infection control lead. What should come with this responsibility?
options: A new job title and a name badge
Training, time and authority to act
A promise of extra pay at appraisal
Keys to the decontamination room
A.why: A lead role needs training to know the standard, protected time and the authority to act.

whyNot.0: A title without training, time or authority sets the person up to fail.
whyNot.2: Pay is a contract matter; it doesn't make the role workable.
whyNot.3: Access alone doesn't give the knowledge or authority the role needs.

B.q: An agency dental nurse arrives to cover for one day. What is most important before they start clinical work?
options: A full read-through of the practice's business plan
A test on dental anatomy and notation
A tour of the staff room and kitchen
A briefing on local procedures and emergency kit
B.why: Visiting staff must know local procedures, where things are and where the emergency equipment is before treating patients.

whyNot.0: The business plan isn't needed to work safely for a day.
whyNot.1: A registered nurse's knowledge is assumed; what they lack is local information.
whyNot.2: Staff facilities matter far less than emergency equipment and procedures.

B.q: You need to check whether a new team member is competent at setting up for an extraction. What is the most reliable evidence?
options: Their own view that they feel confident
Direct observation against an agreed standard
How long they have worked in dentistry
A written reference from their previous employer
B.why: Watching them do the task against an agreed standard is the most reliable evidence of competence.

whyNot.0: Confidence is not the same as competence.
whyNot.2: Experience elsewhere doesn't prove they meet this practice's standard.
whyNot.3: A reference is useful background but isn't direct evidence of the skill.

B.q: During a medical emergency, which leadership style is usually most appropriate?
options: Democratic, asking everyone's opinion first
Laissez-faire, letting each person decide
Directive, one leader giving clear instructions
Consensus, holding a quick vote among the whole team
B.why: In an emergency there is no time for discussion: one leader gives clear instructions and allocates roles.

whyNot.0: Consulting everyone wastes vital time in an emergency.
whyNot.1: Leaving each person to decide causes confusion and gaps.
whyNot.3: A vote delays action when every second counts.

C.q: A practice introduces a new decontamination procedure. What best supports consistent adoption across the team?
options: Emailing it out once and assuming that everyone reads it
Letting each nurse adapt it to suit themselves
Training only the most experienced nurse on site
Training everyone, with the written procedure to hand
C.why: Everyone affected needs training, and the written procedure must be available so practice is consistent and can be checked.

whyNot.0: An email alone doesn't check understanding or change habits.
whyNot.1: Individual versions create inconsistent, unsafe processing.
whyNot.2: Everyone who does the task must be trained, not just one person.

C.q: You are asked to induct a new colleague into decontamination duties. What should the induction cover first?
options: The practice policy and the equipment used
How to fill in the sterilizer log book
How to run the weekly protein residue test
Which sterilizer cycle is quickest to run
C.why: A decontamination induction starts with the practice's policy and the equipment in use, so the detail that follows makes sense.

whyNot.1: Record keeping matters, but it comes after understanding the policy and equipment.
whyNot.2: Periodic tests are taught once the basics are understood.
whyNot.3: Cycle choice depends on the load and validated settings, not speed, and comes later.

C.q: You have a few minutes between patients. Which task is both urgent and important, so should be done first?
options: Updating your CPD log
Restocking used emergency oxygen
Reordering paper towels
Tidying the staff noticeboard
C.why: Emergency equipment must be ready at all times, so replacing used oxygen is urgent and important.

whyNot.0: CPD is important but not urgent; plan time for it.
whyNot.2: Paper towels matter, but running low isn't an immediate risk to life.
whyNot.3: This is neither urgent nor important.

reteach.title: The sat nav and the service schedule
reteach.question: Think about a car journey. Something has to choose the destination and keep everyone motivated, and something has to keep the car serviced and fuelled. Which is leadership and which is management?

blocks.body: Leadership is the sat nav and the driver: it picks where the team is heading, explains why and keeps people on board when the route changes. Management is the service schedule: rotas, stock, maintenance logs and policies that keep the practice running smoothly every day. A team with only management runs well but never improves. A team with only leadership has great ideas but nothing gets done.

rows.label: Explaining why the new hand-hygiene audit matters
Ordering stock and checking expiry dates

explain.body: Leadership is about people, direction and change. Management is about systems, tasks and stability. Dental nurses do both, for example leading a change in practice and managing stock or rotas.

test.q: Which activity is the best example of leadership rather than management?
options: Checking stock expiry dates
Completing the weekly rota
Motivating the team to adopt a change
Logging the daily sterilizer test results
test.why: Motivating people to accept change is about direction and influence, which is leadership.

whyNot.0: Stock checks are a management task.
whyNot.3: Record keeping is a management task.

explain.body: Directive: one person decides; ideal in emergencies. Democratic: the team is consulted; ideal for planning change. Laissez-faire: hands-off; only suits experienced, motivated staff.

test.q: The practice is planning a new appointment system and wants staff to support it. Which leadership style is most likely to help?
options: Directive, with no discussion
Democratic, involving the team
Laissez-faire, leaving it to chance
Avoiding the topic until it's live
test.why: People are more likely to support a change they have helped to shape, so a democratic style suits planned change.

whyNot.0: Imposing change without discussion often meets resistance.
whyNot.2: Leaving it unmanaged means no clear plan.
whyNot.3: Avoiding the topic creates confusion and resentment.

explain.body: New staff: a structured induction with a mentor. Agency or locum staff: a briefing on local procedures and the emergency equipment before clinical work. Sign people off by direct observation against an agreed standard.

test.q: What is the most reliable way to confirm a new nurse is competent at a task?
options: Ask them if they feel ready
Check how long they have been qualified
Assume competence if no one complains
Observe them against an agreed standard
test.why: Direct observation against an agreed standard gives objective evidence of competence.

whyNot.1: Time qualified doesn't prove a specific skill.
whyNot.2: No complaints doesn't mean safe practice.

explain.body: A lead role needs training, time and authority. When a procedure changes, train everyone affected, make the written procedure available and explain why the change matters.

test.q: A nurse is made safeguarding lead but given no training or time for the role. What is the main problem?
options: They can't carry out the role effectively
The role needs a higher job title
Only dentists may hold lead roles
The CQC must approve the appointment
test.why: Without training, time and authority, the person cannot do the lead role properly.

whyNot.1: A title doesn't solve the lack of training or time.
whyNot.2: Dental nurses often hold lead roles.
whyNot.3: The CQC doesn't approve individual lead role appointments.
